name: DRV8801PWPR
title: DRV8800 and DRV8801: 36 V, 2.8 A DMOS full-bridge motor drivers with PHASE/ENABLE control
summary: A single H-bridge of N-channel DMOS switches with an internal charge pump, for one brushed DC motor, one stepper winding or a solenoid, working from 8 V to 36 V at up to 2.8 A peak. PHASE sets direction and ENABLE gates the bridge; MODE pins pick fast or slow decay. Protection covers supply and charge-pump undervoltage, shorts to supply or ground, and over-temperature, reported on an open-drain nFAULT, with a low-power sleep on nSLEEP. The DRV8801 adds a second mode pin and VPROPI, a voltage five times the sense-resistor voltage; the DRV8800 has a VREG test pin instead. DRV8801PWPR is the DRV8801 in 16-pin HTSSOP on a 2000-piece reel.

circuits.title: DRV8801 typical application
circuits.description: One brushed DC motor across OUT+ and OUT-, run from VBB. The controller drives PHASE, ENABLE, MODE 1, MODE 2 and nSLEEP from GPIO lines and reads nFAULT, pulled up to the controller supply by 10 kΩ. A 0.2 Ω resistor from SENSE to ground sets the overcurrent trip at 2.5 A and feeds the current output; VPROPI reaches the controller's ADC through a 100 kΩ and 1000 pF low-pass. The charge pump uses 0.1 µF from CP1 to CP2 and 0.1 µF from VCP to VBB. VBB is decoupled by 0.1 µF ceramic and 100 µF bulk. Both GND pins and the PowerPAD go to ground.
notes: Pin numbers follow the HTSSOP (PWP) package.
The trip current follows RSENSE = 0.5 V / ITRIP: 0.2 Ω gives 2.5 A.

circuits.title: DRV8800 typical application
circuits.description: The DRV8800 version: one brushed DC motor across OUT+ and OUT-, run from VBB. The controller drives MODE, PHASE, nSLEEP and ENABLE and reads nFAULT through a 10 kΩ pull-up to its supply. A 0.2 Ω resistor from SENSE to ground sets the overcurrent trip. The charge pump uses 0.1 µF from CP1 to CP2 and 0.1 µF from VCP to VBB; VBB has 0.1 µF ceramic and 100 µF bulk to ground. A 0.22 µF capacitor from VREG to ground is optional. NC is left open; both GND pins and the PowerPAD go to ground.
notes: Pin numbers follow the HTSSOP (PWP) package.
VREG is otherwise specified to be left unconnected; the 0.22 µF capacitor is marked optional.

circuits.title: RC filter on VPROPI for an ADC
circuits.description: A series 10 kΩ and a 1000 pF capacitor to ground between the VPROPI pin and the microcontroller's ADC input, a low-pass for sampling the current-proportional voltage.

operation.text: Four N-channel DMOS switches form one H-bridge for a brushed DC motor, one stepper winding or a solenoid, at 8 V to 36 V supply and up to 2.8 A peak. PHASE picks the current direction and ENABLE switches the bridge on; when ENABLE is low the bridge recirculates in the decay mode chosen by MODE. 100 % duty cycle is supported. On the DRV8801 a voltage proportional to winding current comes out on VPROPI.

MODE 1 (MODE on the DRV8800) high gives slow decay, low gives fast decay. Slow decay shorts the winding through two switches of the same side, which also brakes the motor. On the DRV8801, MODE 2 chooses the side: high uses the two high-side switches, low the two low-side switches; it has no effect while MODE 1 is low. The DRV8800 slow-decays through the low side. In fast decay, synchronously rectified, the part turns on the opposite pair, as a direction change would, and opens all switches as the current approaches zero so it never reverses. Losses in either decay mode follow the same I² × (source + sink on-resistance) as drive.

nSLEEP low shuts down most of the chip, including the internal rails and the charge pump, and the outputs go high impedance; supply current falls to 10 µA max. nSLEEP high returns to normal operation. After nSLEEP goes high the charge pump and VREG take roughly 200 µs to come up; wait 1 ms before applying PWM so the charge pump has settled. nSLEEP has an internal pull-down.

The charge pump makes a gate supply above VBB for the high-side switches. It needs 0.1 µF ceramic between CP1 and CP2 and a 0.1 µF ceramic storage capacitor from VCP to VBB. VCP is monitored: if it is too low the outputs are disabled until it recovers. Typical VCP rises from about 14 V at VBB = 8 V to about 51 V at VBB = 38 V.

The logic inputs are nSLEEP, MODE (MODE 1, MODE 2), PHASE and ENABLE. More than 7 V on any of them can damage the input. A logic input tied up to VDD should go through a high-value resistor, which limits the input current if VDD overshoots.
VREG carries the internal regulator voltage, about 7.5 V, for measurement only; leave it unconnected. The typical application marks a 0.22 µF capacitor to ground on it as optional.

VPROPI is five times the SENSE voltage, so with a sense resistor it reads winding current for an ADC. It stays at 0 V when SENSE is negative and drops to 0 V during slow-decay recirculation. With SENSE tied straight to ground it outputs 0 V. A series RC (10 kΩ, 1000 pF) is recommended ahead of an ADC; the typical application uses 100 kΩ and 1000 pF.

nFAULT is open drain and goes low on a motor fault, undervoltage or die temperature above 160 °C. It is not valid while nSLEEP is low. At power-up it stays low until VBB reaches VBBNFR (12 V typ, 13.8 V max), leaving the charge pump room to clear its undervoltage threshold. nFAULT only reports: the bridge keeps working with nFAULT low down to VBB = 8 V. Several nFAULT pins can share one pull-up as a wired OR.
UVLO holds the drivers off at power-up until VBB rises past VUV (6.5 V typ, 7.5 V max). A low charge pump voltage also disables the outputs until it is cleared.

Two die-temperature monitors are on chip. At 160 °C a warning pulls nFAULT low but the part keeps running; it clears at 145 °C. At about 175 °C the outputs switch off and stay off until the die has cooled 15 °C. The 2.8 A rating holds only while the die stays below 170 °C. Solder the PowerPAD to the ground plane, with vias through to the outer layers; the design example reaches an effective RθJA of 47 °C/W.

Current through every high-side and low-side switch is monitored for a motor lead shorted to supply or ground. On a short, after the 3 µs deglitch, the bridge turns off, nFAULT goes low and a 1.2 ms timer (tOCP) runs. Then the part follows its inputs again and retries, with nFAULT released for the attempt; if the short is still there the cycle repeats, otherwise normal operation carries on. The internal threshold IOCP is 3 A min.

A low-value resistor from SENSE to ground sets a trip current below the 2.8 A default and, on the DRV8801, provides the VPROPI signal. When SENSE reaches 500 mV the bridge goes high impedance and recirculates as MODE dictates, retrying every tOCP; size the resistor to drop less than 500 mV in normal running, with RSENSE = 500 mV / ITRIP. SENSE tied straight to ground gives 0 V and leaves the 2.8 A maximum. Give the resistor its own short return to the star ground, since PCB IR drop matters with low values; the part wanted is a surface-mount, low-inductance resistor with enough power rating, placed near the driver. Set ITRIP above the running current; start-up current is much higher because of the higher starting torque and no back-EMF. Series inductors on the outputs or a ramped duty cycle limit start-up current, which can allow a lower ITRIP and less bulk capacitance.

Brake by selecting slow decay (MODE 1 high) and taking ENABLE low: the switches conduct both ways and short the motor's back-EMF for as long as ENABLE stays low. The braking current is roughly VBEMF / RL; with fast, high-inertia loads check it stays inside the absolute maximum ratings.

The usual scheme holds PHASE on a GPIO for direction and puts PWM on ENABLE for speed. Alternatively ENABLE is held on a GPIO and PWM goes on PHASE, so one signal sets both speed and direction: 50 % duty stops the motor, above 50 % turns it clockwise with 100 % full speed, below 50 % turns it counter-clockwise with 0 % full speed. ENABLE then only stops the motor and all current. PWM on PHASE and ENABLE is specified up to 100 kHz.
The motor's rating and the speed wanted set VBB. A higher voltage runs the motor faster at the same duty cycle and makes current rise faster in the winding inductance.

Two or more devices of the same type can be paralleled for more than 2.8 A; a DRV8800 should not be paralleled with a DRV8801. Connected in common: ENABLE, PHASE, MODE (MODE 1 and MODE 2 on the DRV8801), nSLEEP, both outputs, SENSE, VBB and GND. VCP, CP1, CP2 and VPROPI are not shared: each device's are wired on their own. Place the devices close together with short traces so their enables stay in step; the protection copes with skew, but full current is there only when every stage is on. Give each device its own sense resistor of the same value so the ITRIP settings match. External Schottky diodes are needed, one from each output to VBB and one from ground to each output, to carry recirculation current during the unsynchronized part of decay, which otherwise all flows in whichever body diode has the lowest forward drop, a diode not built for that current. The total trip current comes out below N × ITRIP because the first device to trip leaves the rest to carry the load; plan on about 90 %.

More local bulk capacitance on VBB is generally better, traded against cost and size. How much depends on the motor system's peak current, the supply's capacitance and current capability, the wiring inductance between supply and driver, the ripple allowed, the motor type and the braking method. Too little lets the supply voltage move when the motor draws or returns current through the wiring inductance. The value has to be confirmed by testing the system.

Use a heavy ground plane and solder the thermal pad directly to exposed copper, with thermal vias to the other layers. Decouple VBB with an electrolytic, typically 100 µF, in parallel with 0.1 µF ceramic close to the device. Place the 0.1 µF capacitors from VCP to VBB and from CP1 to CP2 close to the device. Keep the sense resistor close to SENSE and to its ground return to keep inductance low.
